source: Anchored to public NASA figures where a real unit exists: VIPER rover fact sheet and instrument pages (NSS, NIRVSS, MSolo, TRIDENT; 430 kg rover, 450 W peak solar, 0.72 km/h), the MMRTG fact sheet (about 110 W electric and 2,000 W thermal at launch, 45 kg, plutonium-238 half-life 87.7 years), the NASA Small Spacecraft Technology State-of-the-Art report (solar cell efficiency, battery specific energy, radios, avionics) and NASA flight computer descriptions (RAD750, HPSC). Masses, powers and costs of generic parts are representative values for their class, rounded for gameplay. Mars instruments follow the Perseverance payload (NASA Mars 2020 instrument pages: the coring drill of the Sampling and Caching System, SHERLOC, PIXL, SuperCam, MEDA) and its Electra-Lite UHF relay radio (up to 2 Mbit/s to an orbiter). Small-satellite parts (frames, cells, batteries, wheels, radios, thrusters, imagers) are representative of the classes in the NASA Small Spacecraft Technology State-of-the-Art report; imager swath and resolution follow Landsat-class (30 m, 185 km), Sentinel-2-class (10 m, 290 km from 786 km) and Dove-class (3-4 m, 24 km) instruments scaled to 500 km.
units: mass_kg dry mass; power_w electrical draw while the part is on; cost_musd millions of US dollars; trl NASA technology readiness level 1-9; failure_rate_per_year chance of a disabling fault per year of operation; data_rate_mbps megabits per second averaged over the time the instrument operates (compressed products, not the raw detector rate); max_rate_mbps the ceiling of the radio hardware. speed_m_per_h is the ground a rover covers per hour of driving on average, including the stops to image, plan and check its footing (top speed is far higher: VIPER can do 720 m/h). swath_km_at_500 and gsd_m_at_500 give the ground width imaged and the smallest detail resolved from 500 km (both scale with altitude; 0 for instruments that do not image the ground).

parts.name: Light composite frame
parts.summary: Saves mass on every burn, but carries only a lean set of equipment.

parts.name: Standard aluminium frame
parts.summary: Flight-proven structure with room for a full science payload.

parts.name: Heavy-duty frame
parts.summary: Carries anything in the catalog. Every extra kilogram of frame costs more than a kilogram of propellant to land.

parts.name: Body-mounted solar deck, 2 m²
parts.summary: Cells on the top deck: light, cheap and nothing to deploy. They face the sky, so they only work well where the Sun climbs high.

parts.name: Vertical side panels, 3 × 1 m²
parts.summary: Panels on three sides, like VIPER: whichever way the vehicle turns, one of them faces a Sun that sits on the horizon.

parts.name: Sun-tracking mast array, 6 m²
parts.summary: A tall array that turns to follow the Sun: several times the power, and a new mechanism that has never flown and may slip the schedule.

parts.name: Radioisotope generator (MMRTG)
parts.summary: Plutonium heat turned into about 110 W, day and night, sunlit or not, and its waste heat keeps the vehicle warm. Low power, high price.

parts.name: Lithium-ion battery, 2 kWh
parts.summary: Enough for short dips into shadow. A long night empties it.

parts.name: Lithium-ion battery, 6 kWh
parts.summary: About two days of work in the dark, close to what VIPER carries.

parts.name: Lithium-ion battery, 15 kWh
parts.summary: Big enough to hibernate through a two-week lunar night, at the mass of a whole instrument suite.

parts.name: Hydrazine monopropellant stage
parts.summary: One propellant, few valves, very reliable. Its low exhaust speed means far more propellant for the same manoeuvres.

parts.name: Storable bipropellant stage
parts.summary: Fuel and oxidiser that stay liquid for years. The standard choice for landers: good efficiency, proven hardware.

parts.name: Methane-oxygen stage
parts.summary: The most efficient engine here, with thrust to spare. Its cold propellants boil away in a couple of weeks, so it cannot take the slow route.

parts.name: Sun sensors and gyros
parts.summary: Knows roughly which way is up. Good enough for wide antennas, not for a narrow beam.

parts.name: Star tracker and reaction wheels
parts.summary: Precise pointing: needed to keep a high-gain dish on Earth and to aim narrow instruments.

parts.name: Commercial-grade computer
parts.summary: Fast, light and cheap. A burst of solar radiation can crash it and cost you days.

parts.name: Radiation-hardened computer (RAD750 class)
parts.summary: The processor family that flies on NASA's Mars rovers: slow, with little storage, and it shrugs off solar storms.

parts.name: High-performance spaceflight computer
parts.summary: Hardened and powerful enough to drive and drill without waiting for Earth. New hardware: more cost, more schedule risk.

parts.name: S-band low-gain radio
parts.summary: Talks in every direction at once, slowly. Commands and health data get through; pictures queue up.

parts.name: X-band medium-gain antenna
parts.summary: A wider beam that is easy to keep on Earth, with a useful data rate.

parts.name: X-band steerable high-gain dish
parts.summary: Ten times the data rate through a narrow beam. It needs precise pointing and a clear view of Earth.

parts.name: Lunar relay service link
parts.summary: Pays for passes of a relay satellite in lunar orbit: contact even where Earth is below the horizon, for the price of a subscription.

parts.name: UHF relay radio
parts.summary: Talks to the orbiters that pass overhead a few times a day; their big dishes carry the data to Earth. Megabits instead of kilobits, but only during the passes.

parts.name: Blankets and radiators
parts.summary: Passive insulation. In shadow the heaters must replace all the heat that leaks out.

parts.name: Warm box with louvers and heat switches
parts.summary: Closes itself up in the cold, cutting heater power by about 40 %.

parts.name: Warm box with radioisotope heater units
parts.summary: Small plutonium pellets give free heat for decades. They make a lunar night survivable, and they need nuclear launch approval and money.

parts.name: Four-wheel rover chassis
parts.summary: Simple fixed suspension. It drives on gentle ground only and slowly.

parts.name: Four-wheel steering with active suspension
parts.summary: Every wheel steers and lifts on its own, like VIPER: twice the speed, crater slopes within reach, more mass and power.

parts.name: Radar altimeter landing
parts.summary: Knows its height, not what is underneath. It lands kilometres off target, and polar terrain is full of boulders and long shadows.

parts.name: Terrain-relative navigation
parts.summary: Matches camera images to an onboard map, the method that put Perseverance down within metres of its target.

parts.name: Navigation with hazard-detection lidar
parts.summary: Scans the ground in the last seconds and diverts around rocks. The safest landing; the divert costs propellant and the sensor is new.

parts.name: Neutron spectrometer
parts.summary: Senses hydrogen, the signature of water, up to a metre underground while the rover drives. Tiny, frugal and essential for finding where to drill.

parts.name: Near-infrared spectrometer
parts.summary: Reads the colour of the surface and of drill cuttings to tell water ice from dry minerals.

parts.name: Mass spectrometer
parts.summary: Weighs the gas molecules released by drilling: the proof of what the ice is made of. It needs a drill to feed it.

parts.name: One-metre percussive drill
parts.summary: Brings up cuttings from a metre down, as far as VIPER reaches. Power-hungry while it runs.

parts.name: Two-metre deep drill
parts.summary: Twice the depth, where older ice may lie. Heavy, hungry and unproven: it can jam and it can slip the schedule.

parts.name: Stereo science cameras
parts.summary: Colour panoramas and 3D terrain. Images are the bulkiest data aboard and will fill the recorder unless the downlink keeps up.

parts.name: Ground-penetrating radar
parts.summary: Profiles buried layers along the drive, showing how deep the ice-bearing ground goes.

parts.name: Thermal infrared radiometer
parts.summary: Maps ground temperature to find the cold traps where ice can last for billions of years.

parts.name: Rock coring drill
parts.summary: Cuts a chalk-sized core out of solid rock and seals it in a tube, as Perseverance does. The cores are the mission: everything else decides which rocks deserve one.

parts.name: Ultraviolet Raman spectrometer
parts.summary: Shines an ultraviolet laser on a rock from a few centimetres away and maps organic molecules and the minerals water left behind.

parts.name: X-ray chemistry mapper
parts.summary: Maps the chemical elements across a postage stamp of rock, grain by grain: the texture that tells a lake bed from a lava flow.

parts.name: Laser spectrometer on the mast
parts.summary: Vaporises a pinhead of rock up to seven metres away and reads the flash. It surveys dozens of targets a day without the rover moving.

parts.name: Weather station
parts.summary: Wind, pressure, temperature and dust, day and night: the record future crews will plan around.

parts.name: 12U CubeSat frame
parts.summary: A shoebox-sized standard frame. Cheap and quick to build, with room for one small instrument.

parts.name: Microsatellite frame
parts.summary: The size of a washing machine: room for a real telescope, bigger wheels and a propulsion unit.

parts.name: Small satellite frame
parts.summary: A stiff, well-proven frame for a wide instrument and years of work. It no longer fits the cheapest launch seats.

parts.name: Body-mounted solar cells
parts.summary: Cells glued to the sides of the satellite. Nothing to deploy and nothing to break, but most of them face away from the Sun.

parts.name: Fold-out solar wings
parts.summary: Two panels that spring open after launch. Several times the power; the satellite must turn to face them at the Sun.

parts.name: Sun-tracking solar wings
parts.summary: Wings on motors that follow the Sun while the instrument keeps looking down. The most power, the most drag, and a mechanism that can jam.

parts.name: CubeSat battery pack
parts.summary: Enough for a small satellite through each half-hour of shadow. Batteries cycled fifteen times a day wear out fast, so only part of the charge is used.

parts.name: Small satellite battery
parts.summary: Carries a hungry payload through every eclipse with room to spare.

parts.name: Cold-gas thruster
parts.summary: Compressed gas through a valve. Simple and safe; so inefficient that it can only nudge the orbit.

parts.name: Green monopropellant thruster
parts.summary: A compact chemical thruster that holds the orbit against drag and brings the satellite down at the end.

parts.name: Miniature Hall thruster
parts.summary: Electric propulsion: a whisper of thrust for a sixth of the propellant. It needs a lot of power while it runs.

parts.name: Magnetic torquers
parts.summary: Electromagnets that push against Earth’s magnetic field. They keep the satellite roughly facing down: enough for a wide radio beam, not for a telescope.

parts.name: Reaction wheels and star tracker
parts.summary: Spinning wheels turn the satellite precisely and a star camera tells it where it is looking. Sharp pictures need this; wheels are also what most often fails.

parts.name: CubeSat computer
parts.summary: A phone-class processor with a memory card. Plenty of storage for the price; a solar storm can knock it over.

parts.name: Radiation-tolerant small computer
parts.summary: Rides out radiation without a reset and schedules its own imaging and downlinks.

parts.name: UHF radio
parts.summary: A whip antenna that works in any attitude. Commands and health data only: pictures would take years.

parts.name: S-band radio
parts.summary: A few megabits a second through a patch antenna: fine for a modest camera and a couple of passes a day.

parts.name: X-band downlink
parts.summary: Empties the recorder in a single pass. The narrow beam needs precise pointing and a lot of power while it transmits.

parts.name: Coatings and a small heater
parts.summary: Paint, tape and a thermostat. Earth orbit is gentle: half an hour of shadow at a time.

parts.name: Compact colour imager
parts.summary: Sees cars and field edges through a small telescope. Its narrow strip means the same field comes round only now and then.

parts.name: Wide-swath multispectral imager
parts.summary: Thirteen colour bands across a wide strip: crop health for a whole region in one pass. Heavy, hungry and it floods the downlink.

parts.name: Thermal infrared imager
parts.summary: Measures how warm the ground is: water stress in crops, wildfires, city heat. Coarse detail, and a new detector.

parts.name: Ship-tracking receiver
parts.summary: Listens to the position beacons of ships across a whole ocean at once. Tiny, frugal, and it works in any attitude.

parts.name: Atmosphere sounder (GNSS occultation)
parts.summary: Watches navigation signals bend as they set behind the Earth to profile temperature and moisture for weather forecasts.
